title: No-local-obstruction lemma is neither stated nor proved (needed before any impossibility attempt)

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
For the non-existence direction, the first thing to settle is whether a congruence (mod $m$) obstruction exists. The document does not address this. I verified numerically that for EVERY modulus $m\le 600$ the congruence $\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i^6\equiv z^6\pmod m$ is solvable, so there is NO local obstruction.

Important subtlety: if one wrongly requires the bases coprime to $m$, then $m=3$ and $m=7$ APPEAR to obstruct (mod 7: $x^6\equiv1$ for $7\nmid x$ by Fermat, so five terms sum to $5$, while $z^6\in\{0,1\}$, and $5\notin\{0,1\}\pmod7$). But the bases are arbitrary positive integers and MAY be divisible by 3 or 7, giving residue 0; then $0+0+0+0+z^6\equiv z^6$ is always solvable. So any future 'mod 7 / mod 3 impossibility' argument is INVALID, and local methods cannot prove non-existence. A rigorous write-up should prove this no-obstruction lemma (finite per prime power, lifted by CRT) to document why the elementary impossibility route is closed.

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body: Confirming this gap remains OPEN in the current solution.tex (N=220 revision): no no-local-obstruction lemma is present. Independent verification (this review): the congruence $\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i^6\equiv z^6\pmod m$ is solvable for EVERY modulus $2\le m\le 600$ with bases allowed divisible by $m$. Hence there is no elementary congruence obstruction, and any nonexistence proof must use a non-local argument. The mod-7 'coprime trap' (Fermat gives $x^6\equiv1$ for $7\nmid x$, so five coprime terms give $5\notin\{0,1\}\pmod 7$) is illusory because bases may be multiples of 7. This should be stated and proved explicitly to frame the difficulty.
